title: Perceptual assessment of quality of urban soundscapes with combined noise sources and water sounds
research_focus: To perceptually assess the quality of urban soundscapes containing combined noise sources and water sounds, evaluate annoyance from combined noise sources, and examine the effect of water sounds on masking urban noises to enhance soundscape perception.

sample_context.description: Field surveys: 15 subjects (7 female, 8 male, aged 20–30). Laboratory experiment (individual noise sources): 20 subjects (aged 24-30). Laboratory experiment (natural sounds as maskers): 12 subjects (aged 20-30). Laboratory experiment (water sounds on combined noise sources): 10 subjects (aged 20-30). All participants had normal hearing.
sample_context.setting: Field surveys in 16 urban sites in Seoul and Bundang, Korea (residential areas, open public spaces like streets, parks, squares). Laboratory auditory experiments conducted in a sound-proof testing booth (4x3 m²).

findings.antecedent: Urban soundscape acoustic environment (combined noise sources)
findings.description: Ten semantic adjectives (comfort, quiet, harmonious, soft, monotonous, weak, light, pleasant, unique, warm) were grouped into two components through factor analysis. Component 1 (79% of total variance) related to comfort, loudness, and pitch sensations. Component 2 (15% of total variance) related to temporal variation and common urban soundscapes.

findings.antecedent: Measured sound level (LAeq), Loudness, Annoyance, Acoustic comfort
findings.description: Component 1 (comfort, loudness, pitch sensations) was positively correlated with LAeq (r=0.73, p<0.01), loudness (r=0.93, p<0.01), and annoyance (r=0.91, p<0.01), and negatively correlated with acoustic comfort (r=-0.96, p<0.01). Component 2 (temporal variation, common urban soundscapes) showed negative correlations with LAeq (r=-0.52, p<0.05), loudness (r=-0.59, p<0.05), and annoyance (r=-0.59, p<0.05), and a positive correlation with acoustic comfort (r=0.54, p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Individual noise sources (road traffic, stationary construction, fluctuation construction, intermittent construction, impulsive construction) and their LAeq levels
findings.description: Annoyance ratings for both road traffic and construction noises increased with increasing noise level (LAeq). Road traffic noise was rated slightly higher in annoyance than stationary construction noise (p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Combined noise sources (stationary construction noise + road traffic noise) at varying LAeq levels
findings.description: Total annoyance increased with increasing LAeq of construction noise. When road traffic noise was 55 dBA, combined noise annoyance was significantly higher than the more annoying sound in isolation when construction noise LAeq was 50, 60, 70 dBA (p<0.05). When road traffic noise was 75 dBA, combined annoyance was higher only when construction noise LAeq was 80 dBA (p<0.05); otherwise, it was lower than the more annoying sound (T75) when construction noise levels were lower than road traffic noise (-15 dB).

findings.antecedent: Combined noise sources (impulsive construction noise + road traffic noise) at varying LAeq levels and number of events
findings.description: Total annoyance for impulsive construction noise combined with 55 dBA road traffic noise was significantly higher than the more annoying sound (T55, C60, C70) when construction noise LAeq was 50, 60, 70 dBA (p<0.05). With 75 dBA road traffic noise, combined annoyance was significantly lower than T75 when construction noise LAeq was 60, 70 dBA (p<0.01). The number of nonstationary construction noise events (2, 4, 6) did not significantly affect total annoyance.

findings.antecedent: Various natural sounds (Waterfall, Rainfall, Stream, Waves of lake, Birds in forest, Birds in port, Insects, Bell of church, Wind) combined with urban noises (road traffic, construction noise)
findings.description: Stream and Waves of lake sounds were highly preferred as maskers for both road traffic and construction noises. Rainfall, Birds in port, and Wind showed relatively lower preference.

findings.antecedent: Relative SPL of water sounds (Stream, Waves of lake) compared to urban noises (road traffic, construction noise)
findings.theme_name: Optimal Water Sound Level for Masking
findings.description: Preference was highest when the relative SPL of Stream and Waves of lake was -3 dB compared to road traffic noise. For construction noise, the optimal range was -3 to 0 dB. Preference decreased rapidly when water sound level increased beyond this range.

findings.antecedent: Combined urban noises (road traffic, babble, construction) with varying levels of water sounds
findings.theme_name: Water Sound Enhancement of Combined Urban Noises
findings.description: Preference for combined sources generally decreased with increasing noise level. Water sound at 79 dBA was most effective in enhancing urban soundscape when urban noises (road traffic, babble, construction) varied from 79-82, 69-72, and 81-84 dBA respectively. The effect was highest when water sound level was similar to or slightly less than that of dominant urban noises (not less than 3 dB below urban noises). Positive effects diminished when overall combined noise level was around 90 dBA.

themes_or_constructs: Soundscape Quality Components (Comfort, Quiet, Harmonious, Soft, Weak, Light, Pleasant, Warm, Monotonous, Unique)
Optimal Water Sound Level for Masking
Water Sound Enhancement of Combined Urban Noises
derived_hypotheses: The level of water sounds should be similar to or not less than 3 dB below the level of the urban noises to effectively enhance urban soundscape quality.
mechanism_candidates: Sound masking effect of natural sounds (water sounds) on urban noises (road traffic, construction noises) to improve soundscape perception and reduce annoyance.
transferability_limits: The study was conducted in Seoul and Bundang (Korea) and Sheffield (UK), with subjects aged 20-30. Results may vary across different cultures, age groups, or urban contexts with different dominant noise sources or soundscape characteristics. The study focused on relationships between different sound sources without considering spectral variations in noises at different levels.
limitations: Annoyance responses differed significantly between 5-point verbal and 11-point numerical scales, indicating evaluation scale dependency.
Semantic scales used were not sufficient to distinguish differences between residential and open public soundscapes.
Need for more questions on perception of other sound sources and multicultural research for urban soundscape diversity.
Noise exposure period for nonstationary construction noise was insufficient for awareness of event numbers.
Study did not consider spectral variations in noises at different levels.
Positive effects of water sound diminished when overall combined noise level was around 90 dBA.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In this study, urban soundscapes containing combined noise sources were evaluated through field surveys and laboratory experiments. The effect of water sounds on masking urban noises was then examined in order to enhance the soundscape perception. Field surveys in 16 urban spaces were conducted through soundwalking to evaluate the annoyance of combined noise sources. Synthesis curves were derived for the relationships between noise levels and the percentage of highly annoyed (%HA) and the percentage of annoyed (%A) for the combined noise sources. Qualitative analysis was also made using semantic scales for evaluating the quality of the soundscape, and it was shown that the perception of acoustic comfort and loudness was strongly related to the annoyance. A laboratory auditory experiment was then conducted in order to quantify the total annoyance caused by road traffic noise and four types of construction noise. It was shown that the annoyance ratings were related to the types of construction noise in combination with road traffic noise and the level of the road traffic noise. Finally, water sounds were determined to be the best sounds to use for enhancing the urban soundscape. The level of the water sounds should be similar to or not less than 3 dB below the level of the urban noises.
